15   A.   The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to address certain claims and issues

23        (“Environmental Assessment and Routing Study”) and the factors in Public Utility

 3   Q.   PLEASE EXPLAIN HOW YOUR TESTIMONY RELATES TO THE REBUTTAL

 4        TESTIMONY OF APPLICANTS’ WITNESS MS. KAYLYNNE PHILLIPS.

 5   A.   My rebuttal testimony addresses issues in the testimonies for various intervening

 6        parties regarding the pre-approval routing process and development of, and

 7        conclusions within, the Environmental Assessment and Routing Study.           Ms.

 8        Phillips addresses intervenor testimony related to Applicants’ post-approval

11   Q.   IF YOU DO NOT ADDRESS A SPECIFIC CLAIM IN YOUR REBUTTAL

12        TESTIMONY, DOES THAT INDICATE THAT YOU AGREE WITH OR CONCEDE

13        THE ISSUES RAISED?

15        raised substantially the same environmental and land use concerns related to

18        without listing each individual party who discussed them. While I frequently cite

19        specific intervenor testimonies that articulate those broader concerns, that does

20        not indicate that my response only applies to that party’s concern or that it does

21        not apply equally to the same or similar concerns voiced by other parties.

 3   Q.   SOME           INTERVENORS,   INCLUDING        BONNIE      HELENE       MCANELLY,

 4        INDIVIDUALLY AND AS TRUSTEE OF THE 2025 HOMESTEAD TRUST AND

 5        THE BONNIE HELENE MCANELLY 2023 TRUST (P. 19) INDICATE THAT

 7        PLACE BEFORE CONSTRUCTION ACTIVITIES FOR THE PROPOSED

 8        TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT BEGIN. HOW DO YOU RESPOND?

 9   A.   Surveys and field assessments will be conducted after the Public Utility

10        Commission of Texas (“Commission”) selects a route for the Proposed

11        Transmission Line Project. It is not feasible to conduct detailed biological and other

12        surveys of every proposed alternative link before a final route is selected.

13        Applicants, Halff, and Kimley-Horn do not have right-of-entry to private properties

14        to perform such surveys. Halff and Kimley-Horn’s desktop analysis, in combination

15        with ground and aerial reconnaissance surveys, is standard industry practice for

16        transmission line projects in Texas prior to route finalization. The Commission’s

17        final order will ensure that Applicants have the rights necessary to perform detailed

18        field assessments of the approved route efficiently and cost-effectively. Please

19        see the rebuttal testimony of Ms. Phillips for further details about the timing of

20        environmental field assessments.

22   Q.   CERTAIN INTERVENORS MAKE ARGUMENTS RELATING TO ROUTING

23        FACTORS THE COMMISSION SHOULD CONSIDER, INCLUDING VICTORIA D.

  1        RAY (P. 10) AND JASON A. HOWTON (PP. 21-22).                     WHAT ROUTING

 2        FACTORS MUST THE COMMISSION CONSIDER IN APPROVING THE

 3        PROPOSED TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT?

 4   A.   PURA and 16 TAC § 25.101 provide several routing factors that the Commission

 5        must consider when determining whether to grant a CCN for a new transmission

 6        line. PURA’s routing factors include community values, recreational and park

 7        areas, historical and aesthetic values, and environmental integrity.            The

 8        Commission’s substantive rules require consideration of whether the routes

 9        parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way (“ROW”), including existing

10        transmission facilities, roads, highways, railroads, or telephone utility ROW;

11        whether the routes parallel property lines or other natural or cultural features; and

12        whether the routes conform with the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance,

13        which Commission rules define as “[t]he limiting of exposures to electric and

14        magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and

15        effort.”

16   Q.   WHAT IS THE PRIMARY GOAL OF THE ROUTING PROCESS?

17   A.   The primary goal of the routing process is to identify an adequate number of

18        geographically diverse routes that connect the project’s endpoints, while

19        minimizing the impacts to the study area, as measured by the Commission’s

20        routing factors. The Environmental Assessment and Routing Study quantifies

21        these impacts so the Commission can evaluate the routes and select the route that

22        best meets the requirements of PURA and the Commission’s rules as a whole.

23        Given the range of factors the Commission must consider, this process generally

 2        routing feasibility, and many other factors.

 3   Q.   DO YOU HAVE ANYTHING ELSE TO ADD REGARDING THESE GENERAL

 4        ROUTING CONCERNS?

 5   A.   Yes. Numerous intervenors filed testimony raising concerns about a particular link

 6        or links being located near specific structures, bisecting specific properties, or

 7        diverging from existing compatible corridors. Often, these concerns are factual but

 8        fail to take into consideration the overall routing for the Proposed Transmission

 9        Line Project. While these are valid concerns for the Commission to consider, they

10        often do not account for constraints at other points along the route.

11                 Due to the nature of the study area, all proposed routes at some point will

12        approach habitable structures, deviate from property boundaries, and diverge from

13        existing compatible corridors. This is a necessity of routing almost all transmission

14        lines.    The routing process adopts a holistic view of the proposed routing

15        alternatives and the constraints identified throughout the study area to determine

16        which alternatives best meet the requirements of PURA and the Commission’s

17        substantive rules when taken as a whole. This simply cannot be accomplished by

18        focusing on one link’s impacts to a single property.

  1        PROJECT’S PROXIMITY TO HABITABLE STRUCTURES. DID HALFF AND

 3        PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE ROUTES?

 4   A.   Yes. Several intervenors in this case raised concerns regarding the proximity of

 5        the routes to habitable structures on their property. Halff and Kimley-Horn avoided

 6        routing the Proposed Transmission Line Project near habitable structures where

 7        practical while also balancing the Commission’s other factors, including the need

 8        for an adequate number of reasonably differentiated alternative routes to conduct

 9        a proper evaluation. Prudent avoidance as defined in 16 TAC § 25.101(a)(6)

10        means the limiting of exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided

11        with reasonable investments of money and effort.          My understanding of the

12        Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance is that the process of routing a proposed

13        transmission line should include consideration of routing options that will

14        reasonably avoid population centers and other locations where people gather but

15        also consider costs and other factors.       This does not mean that a proposed

16        transmission line must avoid habitable structures at all costs, but that reasonable

17        alternatives should be considered.

18               To determine the location of habitable structures, Halff and Kimley-Horn

19        reviewed high-resolution aerial imagery and recorded the location of habitable

20        structures potentially located within 520 feet of any link in ArcGIS shapefile format.

21        A distance of 520 feet—rather than 500 feet, as required under Commission

22        rules—was used to provide a buffer to account for photographic interpretation

23        limitations such as shadows, tree canopies, and the margin of error associated

23        feet of each proposed link centerline.

 8        25 years and includes permitting of numerous projects across multiple USACE

20        conclusion that the Proposed Transmission Line Project will exceed the regulatory

21        “fill” thresholds that trigger individual permits. On Bates page 014, Lines 19-20,

22        Ms. Hall states that “NWP 57 covers electric utility and telecommunications line

23        crossings in Waters of the United States.” An important clarification is that NWP
